analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal contracts with for-profit prison companies and adds reentry counseling for released prisoners.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 23, 2025 with 6 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has received no hearing, no vote, and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the federal Bureau of Prisons and the Marshals Service from hiring private, for-profit companies to run their prisons, phasing out existing contracts over six years, with an eight-year timeline for halfway-house-style community confinement facilities. It would require annual inspections of every jail holding federal Marshals Service detainees and direct the government to research what reduces repeat offenses. It would also require that every person leaving federal prison get counseling on clearing their record, finding work, applying for food and health benefits, and registering to vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People held in or moving through federal custody, whose housing and discipline would no longer be a profit center for a private company, and their families. It also serves people leaving federal prison, who would get structured help with expungement, job programs, food and Medicaid applications, ID, and voter registration — steps that reduce the odds of returning to prison.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal prisoners, detainees, and their families

how_it_helps.text: Beginning six years after enactment, all core correctional services — housing, safeguarding, protecting, and disciplining of individuals — at every facility used by the Bureau of Prisons or Marshals Service must be performed by federal government employees, phasing out for-profit contracting [S2].
Eight years after enactment, the Bureau of Prisons may not contract with any for-profit entity to provide or manage community confinement facilities, such as halfway houses [S2].
The Marshals Service must inspect every facility holding its detainees each year to ensure compliance with constitutional, federal, state, and local standards [S2].

Every prisoner released from federal custody must receive information and counseling on expungement rights, employment-barrier programs, vocational and educational rehabilitation, records of completed programs, and help applying for nutrition assistance, Medicaid, Social Security, a driver's license, and voter registration [S2].

The Attorney General must research which community confinement programs and policies improve reintegration and reduce recidivism, and report to Congress on the federal prison population's race, gender, age, nationality, and location of custody every two years [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The private prison companies that hold federal contracts, which would lose that business as the phase-out completes. The federal government would take on the direct cost of housing those prisoners with its own staff, the expense of which is not estimated in the bill text, though the bill gives six to eight years to make the transition.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit prison companies under federal contract

drawbacks.text: The transition is long: existing for-profit contracts could continue for six years for prisons and eight years for community confinement facilities, so companies keep the revenue and the status quo for years after the law would take effect [S2].

The Marshals Service exception lets the government keep contracting with state and local government-run facilities, so some privately staffed or problematic local jails holding federal detainees could remain in use as long as government employees perform core services [S2].

The bill text includes no cost estimate for replacing contracted beds with government-operated, government-staffed facilities, so taxpayers would bear the transition cost without a stated accounting [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real but narrow: ending profit-based operation of federal prisons addresses documented incentives to cut staffing and services for the people inside, and the reentry counseling provisions are concrete help for people leaving prison. The main honest objections are the lengthy phase-out that leaves the current system in place for years, the Marshals exception that preserves government-contracted local facilities, and the absence of a cost estimate for standing up government-run capacity.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which has not scheduled it for a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the End For-Profit Prisons Act of 2025 in the House on May 23, 2025 [S1][S4].

Six Democratic colleagues — Ms. Lee of Pennsylvania, Mrs. McIver, Mr. Johnson of Georgia, Mrs. Ramirez, and Mr. McGovern — joined as original cosponsors, and the bill's cosponsor list totals six, all Democrats [S2][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on May 23, 2025, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no committee action, the private prison companies holding Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service contracts keep their federal business, and the current contracted system continues unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.role: Sponsor, End For-Profit Prisons Act of 2025
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Summer Lee, LaMonica McIver, Hank Johnson, Delia Ramirez, and Jim McGovern
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; the action history shows no committee activity since the May 23, 2025 referral.

against.name: Private prison companies
against.role: Industry holding federal Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service contracts
against.what_they_did: An industry whose revenue depends on operating prisons and detention facilities for the government has an obvious stake in the bill never advancing; no industry opposition appears in the congressional record because the bill never got a hearing.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters — the sponsor and six cosponsors — are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on.

industries.note: The bill eliminates the market for privately operating federal prisons and community confinement facilities, phasing out existing contracts over six to eight years. These companies' revenue comes from housing people the government has incarcerated, so their financial interest runs against the bill's goal of removing profit from imprisonment.

analysis.trajectory: A first-chamber bill with six cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action after referral has rarely advanced on its own; the most likely path is that it sits in the Judiciary Committee until the Congress ends, unless its provisions are folded into a larger justice or appropriations bill.
